meta.title: Who really said "Spread love everywhere you go. Let no one ever come to you without leaving happier"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Mother Teresa — but the popular line is a truncation. The documented wording is "leaving better and happier," first published in a 1998 compilation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Spread love everywhere you go. Let no one ever come to you without leaving happier'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, it's Mother Teresa — but the popular short form drops words. The documented version reads "leaving better and happier," first sourced to a 1998 book.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1910–1997 · Catholic nun & missionary; founder of the Missionaries of Charity
answer.sourceLine: Widely and credibly credited to Mother Teresa — and genuinely rooted in her words. Wikiquote carries a fuller version in its sourced section: “Spread love everywhere you go; first of all in your house … Let no one ever come to you without leaving better and happier,” citing John Templeton’s Worldwide Laws of Life (1998), p. 448. But the tidy popular form — ‘leaving happier’ rather than ‘leaving better and happier,’ with the middle sentences dropped — is a modern truncation, and the earliest documentation is that 1998 compilation, not one of her own books.

source.heading: The source

“… Let no one ever come to you without leaving better and happier.”
“Spread love everywhere you go. Let no one ever come to you without leaving happier” — a truncated form

source.excerpt: Spread love everywhere you go; first of all in your house. Give love to your children, to your wife or husband, to a next door neighbor. Let no one ever come to you without leaving better and happier.
trail: Wikiquote lists the fuller passage in its sourced quotes section, citing John Templeton’s Worldwide Laws of Life (1998), p. 448 — with the wording “leaving better and happier.”
The short popular form circulated on Goodreads reads “leaving happier” and drops the middle sentences — a truncation of the documented passage.
The earliest documentation is a 1998 secondary compilation published just after her death (1997); no primary Mother Teresa book is known to carry this exact popular wording.
source.excerptNote: This is the fuller form recorded in Wikiquote’s sourced section. The popular quote keeps the opening and closing sentences, drops the middle, and shortens ‘better and happier’ to just ‘happier.’
source.rightsHolder: The estate of Mother Teresa / Missionaries of Charity; the earliest documented compilation is © 1998 Templeton Foundation Press.
source.rightsNote: As a twentieth-century statement (Mother Teresa died in 1997) first documented in a 1998 compilation, this text is well after the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff and should be treated as in copyright — controlled by her estate/order and the compilation’s publisher. The exact popular short form is a later truncation of uncertain precise provenance, which is a further reason not to treat it as free of rights.

author.name: Mother Teresa
author.heading: About Mother Teresa
author.metaLine: 1910–1997 · Catholic nun & missionary; founder of the Missionaries of Charity
author.bio: Mother Teresa (born Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu in Skopje) was an Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta in 1950 and spent decades serving the poor, sick, and dying. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 and was canonized as Saint Teresa of Calcutta in 2016. Her counsel on love, kindness, and service is among the most quoted — and most freely paraphrased — of the twentieth century.

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but altered in circulation
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong author: the passage really is Mother Teresa’s. What travels online, however, is a shortened and reworded version of what she actually said.

items.why: The documented passage ends “leaving better and happier”; the popular quote clips this to “leaving happier” and omits the middle sentences about loving those in your own home, per Wikiquote’s sourced text.

items.who: John Templeton, Worldwide Laws of Life (1998)
items.why: The earliest documentation Wikiquote gives is Templeton’s 1998 compilation (p. 448) — a book about her words, not one of her own published works, so the precise primary origin of the line is not pinned down.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and most of the wording are authentically Mother Teresa’s; the widely shared short form is a modern truncation whose earliest documentation is a 1998 compilation, not a primary source.

context.heading: A kindness passage, smoothed for sharing
lead: Mother Teresa returned again and again to the idea that kindness should leave a visible mark on everyone we meet. The fuller passage — “Spread love everywhere you go … Let no one ever come to you without leaving better and happier” — sits alongside her well-known lines about being “the living expression of God’s kindness: kindness in your face, kindness in your eyes, kindness in your smile.”

As the sentiment spread across quote sites and social media, it was smoothed into a punchier couplet: the interior sentences fell away and ‘better and happier’ became simply ‘happier.’ The result reads well on a poster, but it is a paraphrase of what she is documented as saying.
context.pull: “Let no one ever come to you without leaving better and happier.”
